scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study (retrospective EHR cohort of 457,950 COVID-19 patients across 58 hospitals) measures postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC/Long COVID) prevalence, chronicity, organ-system heterogeneity, and surveillance gaps; Lyme disease is not mentioned anywhere in the document body.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This JAMA Network Open study used an AI phenotyping algorithm (P2RC) on electronic health record data from 58 hospitals in 4 US regions (2017-2025) to estimate how many COVID-19 patients actually develop Long COVID (PASC), compared with how many are captured by standard diagnostic codes. Among 457,950 COVID-19 patients, the algorithm identified PASC in 16.28% overall (ranging 13.64%-22.69% by region), more than double the <7% typically found using code-based surveillance. Of those with PASC, 89.31% had developed a chronic condition requiring ongoing management, equal to 14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort, and PASC prevalence was still increasing (not resolving) through mid-2024 in three of the four regions. The study reports no direct dollar costs, out-of-pocket spending, lost income, or caregiver-time figures of its own; it cites other studies' cost/utilization estimates for context only.

contextual_issues: Elevated health care utilization among PASC patients, including higher hospitalization odds (OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.23-1.33), is mentioned in the Introduction but is cited from an external study (ref 5), not measured in this cohort.

PASC patients are cited as generating approximately 1.5 times higher health care costs than matched controls (refs 37-38) in the Discussion, but this is an external citation, not a cost figure produced by this study's own data.

Fragmented, cross-specialty care-seeking is described qualitatively (patients presenting to primary care, cardiology, endocrinology, neurology under alternative diagnostic codes with no connecting code to antecedent infection), but the document provides no counts of visits, time-to-diagnosis, or associated cost for this fragmentation.

Background meta-analytic prevalence/persistence figures cited in the Introduction (43% overall PASC prevalence; 45% unresolved symptoms at ~4 months; 30% persistent at 24 months) are drawn from other studies (refs 13, 14, 18, 19), not this cohort's own findings.
No direct medical costs, out-of-pocket costs, lost income/productivity, paid caregiving help, or insurance/access barriers for PASC patients are quantified anywhere in this document.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, lost-income, or productivity-loss data are reported; monetizing this burden would require linking this cohort (or a comparable one) to claims or cost-accounting data such as MEPS.

No COVID-19-negative comparator group was included, so excess incidence of chronic disease attributable to COVID-19 versus background rates cannot be quantified (acknowledged as a limitation by the authors).

Site-specific EHR chart-review validation (precision/recall) was performed only via distributional robustness testing, not direct chart review, at 3 of the 4 regions (Southeast Texas, Southern California, Western Pennsylvania), per the Limitations section.

The 'loyalty score' filter selects for patients with more complete longitudinal documentation, so individuals with limited or fragmented health care engagement are likely underrepresented, meaning the reported prevalence may itself understate true community burden.

PASC incidence/prevalence rates (as opposed to case demographic composition) are not disaggregated by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, veteran status, or other protected categories relative to each subgroup's own denominator.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool this cohort's phenotyping-derived regional prevalence (13.64%-22.69%, observed in a 4-region, 58-hospital EHR cohort using validated AI phenotyping, 2017-2025) with the cited code-based national surveillance estimate (<7%, drawn from external claims/ICD-10-code studies, refs 16-17) as a single low-to-high confidence range - they differ in population, case-ascertainment method, and are explicitly described by the authors as not directly compared head-to-head in this study.

The 4 regional cohorts differ enormously in sample size (5,002 COVID-19 cases in Southeast Texas vs. 252,649 in Western Pennsylvania) and demographic composition (e.g., Western Pennsylvania mean age 47.4 years vs. ~57-58 years in the other 3 regions); do not average or rank them as directly comparable estimates of one quantity without noting this structural heterogeneity.

The compounded '13% to 81% relative increase' decade-long projection (Discussion, p.8) applies only to the three regions with statistically significant quarterly IRR trends (New England, Southern California, Western Pennsylvania); Southeast Texas's quarterly trend did not reach statistical significance (IRR 1.00, 95% CI 1.00-1.01, P=.07) and must not be folded into that projected range.

spec.title: Long COVID (PASC) Prevalence and Chronic-Conversion Simulator
spec.boundary: This simulation represents prevalence, chronic-conversion, and surveillance-gap findings from a single 58-hospital, 4-region EHR cohort study (457,950 COVID-19 patients, 2017-2025) using an AI phenotyping algorithm (P2RC). It omits all direct medical costs, out-of-pocket spending, lost income, caregiver time, and health care utilization, none of which this document measures in its own cohort (those figures only appear as external citations for context). The national extrapolation output is explicitly flagged by the study authors as needing cautious interpretation, not a validated count.

takeaway.patient: In this large hospital-records study, an AI-based symptom-pattern detection method found Long COVID in about 1 in 6 people who had COVID-19 - more than double the share typically identified using standard diagnosis codes alone. Of people identified this way, almost 9 in 10 went on to have a lasting health condition needing ongoing management, not a short-term illness that resolved on its own. This suggests standard medical coding may miss many people whose ongoing symptoms are connected to a past COVID-19 infection.
takeaway.care: Using AI-based phenotyping rather than diagnosis codes alone, this cohort found PASC in 16.28% of COVID-19 patients (range 13.64%-22.69% across 4 regions), more than double the under-7% typically captured by code-based surveillance, and 89.31% of identified PASC patients went on to develop a chronic condition requiring ongoing management. The study also describes these patients being seen across primary care, cardiology, endocrinology, and neurology under separate diagnosis codes with no shared code linking presentations back to the antecedent infection, and organ-system patterns differed significantly by region.
takeaway.policy: This EHR-based phenotyping study estimates PASC prevalence at 16.28% of COVID-19 patients (regional range 13.64%-22.69%), versus a cited code-based surveillance estimate of under 7% - a gap the authors attribute partly to known limits of ICD-10/claims-based case capture. 89.31% of identified PASC cases (14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort) involved a chronic condition requiring ongoing management, and prevalence was still rising through mid-2024 in 3 of 4 regions. An extrapolation to ~15 million US individuals is offered by the authors only as an illustrative, caution-flagged figure, not a validated national count.

patient: If you have ongoing symptoms after COVID-19 (fatigue, new heart-rate changes, new blood-sugar issues, cognitive changes), consider asking your clinician whether these could be connected to a post-COVID chronic condition, even if no single diagnosis code currently links them together.

If you are seeing several different specialists for symptoms that started after a COVID-19 infection, consider keeping your own timeline connecting them, since this study found such presentations are often not linked in medical records.

If you are pursuing a disability or insurance claim related to long-term post-COVID symptoms, this study's finding that most identified cases became chronic may be useful evidence to raise with your advocate or caseworker.

Discuss with a patient advocacy group whether this study's finding - that standard diagnosis coding likely undercounts Long COVID - is relevant to how your case or community's cases are being recognized.
care: This finding - that coded PASC surveillance may capture under half of phenotyping-identified cases - may be worth checking against your own site's coding and referral patterns for post-COVID patients.

Consider whether patients presenting separately to cardiology, endocrinology, neurology, or primary care with new-onset symptoms after a documented COVID-19 infection are being linked back to that infection in the record, given the fragmentation this study describes.

Use the region-specific organ-system heterogeneity findings as a prompt to review which specialty services in your own system may be seeing rising, uncoordinated referral volumes tied to unlabeled post-COVID conditions.
Since prevalence was still increasing through mid-2024 in three of four regions studied, consider whether current chronic-care capacity planning assumes PASC caseloads have stabilized.
policy: Use the gap between phenotyping-identified prevalence and code-based surveillance estimates to model how much chronic post-COVID care demand may be under-recognized in claims-based planning, while treating the exact multiplier as cohort-specific rather than a national constant.

Consider whether reimbursement and disability-determination frameworks that rely on existing diagnosis codes for Long COVID may need review, given this study's finding that most identified cases involved a chronic condition requiring ongoing management.

Treat the ~15 million national extrapolation as an illustrative, author-flagged estimate rather than a confirmed count when using it in planning documents, and consider commissioning validation against claims or survey data (e.g., MEPS) before relying on it for budgeting.

Evaluate whether surveillance infrastructure investment (e.g., adding a code connecting specialty presentations to antecedent COVID-19 infection) could address the coordination gap this study describes.

## Source and scope
This simulator is built from a JAMA Network Open retrospective EHR cohort study (457,950 COVID-19 patients, 58 hospitals, 4 US regions, 2017-2025) using an AI phenotyping algorithm (P2RC) to identify Long COVID / PASC. All prevalence and chronic-conversion figures are the study's own observed cohort findings; the code-based surveillance comparator (under 7%) and the national case count (~103 million) are external figures the authors cite for context, not measured in this cohort.

## Limitations
**Claims/coding undercounting:** The under-7% code-based surveillance comparator comes from external ICD-10/claims-based studies (refs 16-17); the authors state they relied on published estimates of diagnosis-code sensitivity rather than measuring site-specific code counts directly, so that figure likely undercounts the true burden relative to phenotyping-based detection.

**No subgroup-specific rates:** Overall and chronic PASC prevalence are broken out by region, and PASC case demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity) are reported, but the document does not report PASC prevalence rates computed separately by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, or disability status relative to each subgroup's own COVID-19 case denominator. The pooled prevalence and chronic-conversion figures here have not been checked for such variation; federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it.

**Systemic evidence gap:** The study describes patients with chronic postviral conditions presenting separately to primary care, cardiology, endocrinology, and neurology under diagnosis codes with no connecting code back to the antecedent COVID-19 infection, which the authors say impedes both surveillance and coordinated clinical management - a limitation of the diagnostic-coding and care-coordination system itself, distinct from the accuracy of the burden estimates above.

**Sex-based finding:** PASC patients were more likely to be female than the overall COVID-19 population in all four regions (roughly 60%-66% female among PASC cases vs. 60.07% female overall), reported by the authors as a direct comparison rather than a quantified effect size.

## What this simulator omits
No direct medical costs, out-of-pocket spending, lost income, or caregiver-time figures are reported anywhere in this document; this tool cannot answer financial what-if questions. No COVID-19-negative comparator group was used, so excess chronic-disease incidence attributable to COVID-19 versus background rates cannot be quantified from this study alone.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Overall PASC (Long COVID) prevalence identified via AI phenotyping (P2RC) among COVID-19 patients across 4 US regions (2020-2024): the document reports 16.28% as the share of adults who ever had COVID-19 that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 27 wave(s) in that period ranged from 25.6% to 35.1% (interval bounds 24.9% to 36%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.

spec.title: Long COVID (PASC) Prevalence and Chronic-Conversion Simulator
spec.boundary: This simulation represents prevalence, chronic-conversion, and surveillance-gap findings from a single 58-hospital, 4-region EHR cohort study (457,950 COVID-19 patients, 2017-2025) using an AI phenotyping algorithm (P2RC). It omits all direct medical costs, out-of-pocket spending, lost income, caregiver time, and health care utilization, none of which this document measures in its own cohort (those figures only appear as external citations for context). The national extrapolation output is explicitly flagged by the study authors as needing cautious interpretation, not a validated count.

takeaway.patient: In this large hospital-records study, an AI-based symptom-pattern detection method found Long COVID in about 1 in 6 people who had COVID-19 - more than double the share typically identified using standard diagnosis codes alone. Of people identified this way, almost 9 in 10 went on to have a lasting health condition needing ongoing management, not a short-term illness that resolved on its own. This suggests standard medical coding may miss many people whose ongoing symptoms are connected to a past COVID-19 infection.
takeaway.care: Using AI-based phenotyping rather than diagnosis codes alone, this cohort found PASC in 16.28% of COVID-19 patients (range 13.64%-22.69% across 4 regions), more than double the under-7% typically captured by code-based surveillance, and 89.31% of identified PASC patients went on to develop a chronic condition requiring ongoing management. The study also describes these patients being seen across primary care, cardiology, endocrinology, and neurology under separate diagnosis codes with no shared code linking presentations back to the antecedent infection, and organ-system patterns differed significantly by region.
takeaway.policy: This EHR-based phenotyping study estimates PASC prevalence at 16.28% of COVID-19 patients (regional range 13.64%-22.69%), versus a cited code-based surveillance estimate of under 7% - a gap the authors attribute partly to known limits of ICD-10/claims-based case capture. 89.31% of identified PASC cases (14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort) involved a chronic condition requiring ongoing management, and prevalence was still rising through mid-2024 in 3 of 4 regions. An extrapolation to ~15 million US individuals is offered by the authors only as an illustrative, caution-flagged figure, not a validated national count.

patient: If you have ongoing symptoms after COVID-19 (fatigue, new heart-rate changes, new blood-sugar issues, cognitive changes), consider asking your clinician whether these could be connected to a post-COVID chronic condition, even if no single diagnosis code currently links them together.

If you are seeing several different specialists for symptoms that started after a COVID-19 infection, consider keeping your own timeline connecting them, since this study found such presentations are often not linked in medical records.

If you are pursuing a disability or insurance claim related to long-term post-COVID symptoms, this study's finding that most identified cases became chronic may be useful evidence to raise with your advocate or caseworker.

Discuss with a patient advocacy group whether this study's finding - that standard diagnosis coding likely undercounts Long COVID - is relevant to how your case or community's cases are being recognized.
care: This finding - that coded PASC surveillance may capture under half of phenotyping-identified cases - may be worth checking against your own site's coding and referral patterns for post-COVID patients.

Consider whether patients presenting separately to cardiology, endocrinology, neurology, or primary care with new-onset symptoms after a documented COVID-19 infection are being linked back to that infection in the record, given the fragmentation this study describes.

Use the region-specific organ-system heterogeneity findings as a prompt to review which specialty services in your own system may be seeing rising, uncoordinated referral volumes tied to unlabeled post-COVID conditions.
Since prevalence was still increasing through mid-2024 in three of four regions studied, consider whether current chronic-care capacity planning assumes PASC caseloads have stabilized.
policy: Use the gap between phenotyping-identified prevalence and code-based surveillance estimates to model how much chronic post-COVID care demand may be under-recognized in claims-based planning, while treating the exact multiplier as cohort-specific rather than a national constant.

Consider whether reimbursement and disability-determination frameworks that rely on existing diagnosis codes for Long COVID may need review, given this study's finding that most identified cases involved a chronic condition requiring ongoing management.

Treat the ~15 million national extrapolation as an illustrative, author-flagged estimate rather than a confirmed count when using it in planning documents, and consider commissioning validation against claims or survey data (e.g., MEPS) before relying on it for budgeting.

Evaluate whether surveillance infrastructure investment (e.g., adding a code connecting specialty presentations to antecedent COVID-19 infection) could address the coordination gap this study describes.

outputs.label: Phenotyping-identified prevalence minus code-based surveillance estimate (positive = AI phenotyping found more PASC than code-based surveillance; negative = code-based surveillance found more)
outputs.interpretation: This shows how much higher the study's own AI-phenotyping prevalence estimate is than the external code-based surveillance figure it cites for context. The study describes these as measuring different things (validated algorithmic phenotyping in one cohort vs. diagnosis-code capture in external studies) and states they were not directly compared head-to-head; a larger value here illustrates the scale of that difference, not a validated single 'true' prevalence.

outputs.label: Chronic PASC prevalence as a share of all COVID-19 patients
outputs.interpretation: This combines the overall phenotyping-identified PASC rate with the share of those cases that became chronic, reproducing the study's own reported 14.54% chronic-PASC share of all COVID-19 patients. A higher value means a larger share of all COVID-19 patients in this cohort ended up with a lasting condition requiring ongoing management, not just a transient post-infection phase.

outputs.label: Southern California prevalence minus Western Pennsylvania prevalence (positive = Southern California higher; negative = Western Pennsylvania higher)
outputs.interpretation: This shows the size of the regional difference in phenotyping-identified PASC prevalence between the study's highest- and lowest-prevalence regions. The study notes these two regional cohorts differ substantially in size and age composition, so this gap reflects real reported regional variation rather than a ranking of measurement accuracy.

outputs.label: Illustrative national extrapolation of chronic PASC individuals
outputs.interpretation: This applies this cohort's own chronic-PASC share to an external national COVID-19 case count, reproducing the study's illustrative ~15 million figure at default settings. The authors explicitly flag this extrapolation as needing cautious interpretation because the cohort requires longitudinal EHR documentation and excludes certain preexisting-condition patients; it should not be treated as a validated national count.
